clue.text: Incomplete English edition of Othello put up: it's likely to cost extra

indicators.note: a new edition is a reworked version, so the shortened word comes out in a new order
in a down clue, putting something up means writing it from bottom to top

blocks.note: the word English with its last letter cut off
Othello is the Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: A publisher warns that a cut-down English printing of Shakespeare's Othello will be pricey.
explanation.walkthrough: Hotels in Britain commonly charge a single supplement, so a room for one person costs extra per head.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotels often add a supplement when one guest occupies a bedroom alone, making this the pricier option.

clue.text: Beautiful lady's alias, an outrage with tree for city

indicators.note: one thing given for another means a swap: the named word takes the place of the other inside the outrage word

blocks.note: an atrocity is a shocking outrage
taken as written; this is the part taken out
a pine is a tree; this goes in its place

explanation.surface: A lady's nickname is described as a scandal, with an odd swap of tree for city.
explanation.walkthrough: Belladonna is Italian for 'beautiful lady' and is the deadly nightshade plant, whose poison goes by another name. 'with tree for city' is the swap instruction, not part of the surface story.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropine is the toxic alkaloid extracted from deadly nightshade, whose plant name means beautiful lady in Italian.

clue.text: "This was a man", not a beast, almost American

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of it, so the final letter of the beast word is dropped

blocks.note: a brute is a beast
US is the usual abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A tribute insisting the dead man was human, not an animal, and nearly an American.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony's closing words in Julius Caesar praise the conspirator: 'Nature might stand up and say to all the world, This was a man!'
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony speaks these words over the body of the conspirator at the end of Shakespeare's Julius Caesar.

clue.text: Comic writer's tragedy

blocks.note: first meaning: Edward, the Victorian author of nonsense verse and limericks
second meaning: Shakespeare's play about an old king and his daughters

explanation.surface: A humorous author has suffered some misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests the writer owns the tragedy; in fact the funny man and Shakespeare's king share a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear wrote nonsense poems such as The Owl and the Pussycat, and King Lear is a Shakespeare tragedy.

clue.text: Practises economy in relation to World War I scene

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
the Western Front's dug-in lines were the defining scene of the 1914-18 war

explanation.surface: Someone cuts spending in connection with the Western Front of 1914-18.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut back spending and reduce costs is to economise, the verb's financial sense.

clue.text: Promoter of togetherness between a Lapp and a Russian

indicators.note: the letters sit in the gap spanning the following words rather than being built from their meanings

blocks.note: the run starts at the last letter of the Sami word and ends partway into the nationality

explanation.surface: Someone fosters friendship between a Sami person and a Russian.
explanation.walkthrough: In Troilus and Cressida this Trojan arranges the lovers' meeting; his name gave English the word 'pander'.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the go-between who brings the two lovers together in Shakespeare and Chaucer, a matchmaker and procurer.

clue.text: Past ending, a short name and a bad one holding it, in 4

indicators.note: holding it means the bad name wraps around the short name just mentioned

blocks.note: -ed is the ending that turns a verb into its past tense
a bad name: if your name is mud you are in disgrace
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A grammarian's note about tense endings and bad names, pointing to the earlier clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 refers to 4 down, King Lear; this character is the scheming illegitimate son of Gloucester in that play, so 'a bad one' also hints at him.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund is the treacherous bastard son of the Earl of Gloucester in Shakespeare's King Lear.

clue.text: See 23
Put the said seed in the ground and pray for it

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word that follows stands for another one heard the same

blocks.note: with 'Put' before it, this is the phrase for burying, and to inter is to bury
a verb meaning yield or give up, pronounced identically

explanation.surface: A gardener sows seed, then prays for it to grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put ... in the ground' is split by the homophone, which sits inside the burial phrase in the surface but follows it in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To intercede is to plead with a higher power on behalf of someone or something else.

clue.text: Divine in liquor? That's bad

indicators.note: in places the clergyman's letters inside the drink

blocks.note: ale is a malt liquor
a divine is a theologian, and DD is Doctor of Divinity

explanation.surface: A clergyman found in drink: a disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' looks like an adjective or verb but is a noun for a cleric. Addle as an adjective means rotten, as in an addle egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Addle is an old adjective for rotten or spoiled, used of eggs that fail to hatch.

clue.text: Richard III briefly (note missing queen) and 7 still more briefly

blocks.note: first meaning: before he took the crown Richard was Duke of Gloucester, and the shorter spelling is how the early texts give it
second meaning: the answer to 7 down ends King Lear holding his father's earldom, so the title is his too

explanation.walkthrough: Gloucester is pronounced in two syllables, and the old Folio spelling drops the silent letters. The bracketed remark is a teasing aside; 7 down is Edmund, made Earl in Lear.
explanation.definitionFit: Both Shakespeare's Richard of York and the earldom in King Lear carry this title, spelt as the pronunciation suggests.

clue.text: Turn out, maybe, to the credit of Kipling's dhole (without the H)?

definitions.text: Turn out, maybe, to the credit

indicators.note: without means leaving out the letter named in the bracket

blocks.note: in The Second Jungle Book the dholes are the 'Red Dog' pack, wild red hounds
taken as written; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: Asking whether something counts in favour of the wild dog from Kipling's jungle stories, minus a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'turn out to the credit', the idiom 'redound to someone's credit'; 'maybe' flags it as loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that redounds to your credit turns out to benefit or bring honour to you.

clue.text: Prophet like "Tales from Shakespeare"?

blocks.note: first meaning: the Greek and New Testament form of the name Elijah
second meaning: belonging to Charles Lamb's pen name, since he co-wrote those retellings

explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb signed his essays Elia; read with an apostrophe, the answer means 'by Elia', as Tales from Shakespeare was.
explanation.definitionFit: Elias is the New Testament spelling of the Old Testament prophet Elijah, and also the possessive of Lamb's essay pseudonym.

clue.text: For children at the fete among lots of lions? On your head be it!

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter
among means placed in the middle of the group of lions

blocks.note: a group of lions is a pride
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fete attraction staged among big cats; the organiser takes full responsibility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your head be it!' reads as an idiom of warning, but it is split into pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Short rides on small horses are a traditional children's attraction at British village fetes and fairs.

clue.text: Matters of precedence between a religious man and one with family connections

blocks.note: a prior heads a priory of monks
I is the Roman numeral for one
family ties are the bonds of kinship

explanation.surface: A question of rank arising between a monk and someone well connected.
explanation.definitionFit: Priorities are the things judged most important, given precedence over all others.

clue.text: Sept 1: is MCC playing? There's doubt

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are in action and moving about, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the digit one looks like the letter I
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cricket fans wonder whether the MCC side will take the field on the first of September.
explanation.walkthrough: MCC is the Marylebone Cricket Club, the historic owner of Lord's cricket ground in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Scepticism is a questioning attitude, an unwillingness to believe claims without proof.

clue.text: Following a clue to the Globe: Hamlet, Timon, Nym, Nerissa, Pansy, Pia - we've got muddled

annotation.answer: ONE MAN IN HIS TIME PLAYS MANY PARTS

definitions.text: Following a clue to the Globe

indicators.note: muddled means jumbled up, so the listed names are thrown together and remade

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A roll call of characters for a Globe production has got hopelessly mixed up.
explanation.walkthrough: The Globe theatre's motto, roughly 'all the world plays the actor', points to Jaques's speech in As You Like It beginning 'All the world's a stage'; this line follows soon after.
explanation.definitionFit: In As You Like It, Jaques's speech that opens with the world as a stage continues with this line about each man's roles.

clue.text: Assess value and supply information about article

indicators.note: about means going around, so the informing verb surrounds the article

blocks.note: to apprise someone is to inform them
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A valuer prices an item and writes up details about it.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise something is to estimate its worth, as an expert does with antiques or property.

clue.text: Article on Coriolanus with missing sections, a peri-ed piece?

indicators.note: sections missing means parts at each end of the play's title are cut away
in a down clue, one thing on another sits below it, so the article is written after the trimmed play

blocks.note: Shakespeare's Roman tragedy, taken as written before trimming
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: An essay on Shakespeare's Coriolanus with gaps, offered as a costume drama.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed below. A peri is a fairy, and this Gilbert and Sullivan opera is subtitled The Peer and the Peri; 'peri-ed piece' puns on period piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Iolanthe is the Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera about a fairy, or peri, and the House of Lords.

clue.text: See 16
Working on my own radar, I didn't need RADA

indicators.note: working means in motion and being processed, so the letters are moved around

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A self-taught actor boasts of following his instincts rather than going to drama school.
explanation.walkthrough: RADA is London's Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. The actor, born in London and raised in Ireland, learned his craft on the Dublin stage, not at drama school.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Rodway, the Shakespearean actor, began on stage in Dublin after Trinity College rather than training at the London academy.

clue.text: Some more letters to secure a new tenant

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the following words is used

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A landlord writes extra letters to find a new occupant.
explanation.definitionFit: To relet a property is to rent it out again, finding a fresh occupant after the last one leaves.

clue.text: See 20
Fruit went off quickly, in brief

indicators.note: in places the hurried departure inside the word for brief

blocks.note: curt means short or abrupt
ran means went away fast

explanation.surface: Some fruit went bad fast, to put it shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went off' suggests fruit going rotten, but here it means departing.
explanation.definitionFit: A currant is a small dried grape, or a berry such as blackcurrant.

clue.text: Ape making little noise in military unit

indicators.note: in places the quiet letter inside the abbreviated unit

blocks.note: Coy is the military abbreviation for company
p is piano, the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A monkey creeps quietly into an army company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' looks like the animal, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to imitate or mimic them, like a monkey copying people.

clue.text: Language spoken in Alnwick and the south of France

indicators.note: spoken points to how the town's name is pronounced rather than how it is written

blocks.note: sud is French for south
the Northumberland town's name is said with silent l and w

explanation.surface: Some tongue heard both in a northern English town and in Provence.
explanation.walkthrough: Alnwick is a castle town in Northumberland, England, said as 'Annick'. 'The south of France' looks like the region, but it is the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudanic denotes a group of African languages spoken across the Sudan belt south of the Sahara.

clue.text: Joycean role with movement gracious as in the old days

blocks.note: a step is a movement of the foot

blocks.clueFragment: gracious as in the old days
blocks.note: an archaic word for courteous or gracious

explanation.surface: A part in a Joyce adaptation calling for graceful, old-fashioned movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen D is Hugh Leonard's 1962 stage version of Joyce's Portrait of the Artist, whose title role Norman Rodway created.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen D is the title character of the play adapted from Joyce's novels, Stephen Dedalus under a shortened name.

clue.text: See 16
Solvers in line for cricket trophy - for batting?

indicators.note: in places the solvers' word inside the railway line

blocks.note: the El is the elevated railway line in Chicago and once New York
ye is the old plural you, addressing the solvers
the urn contested in England v Australia Test cricket

explanation.surface: Crossword fans queue for a famous cricket trophy, perhaps hoping to bat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batting' looks like cricket, but people bat their lashes when flirting. The Ashes is the trophy for Test series between England and Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Flirts flutter or bat their lashes, the hairs fringing the lids, so these are what one bats.
